claim: Dystroglycan is a cell membrane receptor that organizes the basement membrane by binding ligands in the extracellular matrix.
source: Dystroglycan is a cell membrane receptor that organizes the basement membrane by binding ligands in the extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the function of dystroglycan, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Proper glycosylation of the α-dystroglycan (α-DG) subunit is essential for dystroglycan's activities.
source: Proper glycosylation of the α-dystroglycan (α-DG) subunit is essential for these activities
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Lack of proper α-DG glycosylation results in neuromuscular disease.
source: lack thereof results in neuromuscular disease
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: FKRP, FKTN, TMEM5 and B4GAT1 localize to the Golgi.
source: Here we show that FKRP, FKTN, TMEM5 and B4GAT1 (formerly known as B3GNT1) localize to the Golgi
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating co-localization with Golgi marker Giantin.

claim: FKRP, FKTN, TMEM5 and B4GAT1 contribute to the O-mannosyl post-phosphorylation modification of α-DG.
source: Here we show that FKRP, FKTN, TMEM5 and B4GAT1 (formerly known as B3GNT1) localize to the Golgi and contribute to the O-mannosyl post-phosphorylation modification of α-DG.
evidence: This is supported by phosphorylation assays shown in Figure 1A and complementation studies in Figure 1C.

claim: B4GAT1 functions as a xylose β1,4-glucuronyltransferase.
source: Moreover, we assigned B4GAT1 a function as a xylose β1,4-glucuronyltransferase.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro enzyme assays (Figure 3) and NMR structural analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: A glucuronic acid β1,4-xylose disaccharide synthesized by B4GAT1 acts as an acceptor primer that can be elongated by LARGE with the ligand-binding heteropolysaccharide.
source: Nuclear magnetic resonance studies confirmed that a glucuronic acid β1,4-xylose disaccharide synthesized by B4GAT1 acts as an acceptor primer that can be elongated by LARGE with the ligand-binding heteropolysaccharide.
evidence: This is supported by NMR structural analysis of the tetrasaccharide product shown in Figure 7.

claim: Mutations in B4GAT1 disrupt dystroglycan function and cause disease.
source: Our findings greatly broaden the understanding of α-DG glycosylation and provide mechanistic insight into why mutations in B4GAT1 disrupt dystroglycan function and cause disease.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that B4GAT1 mutations affect enzyme activity (Figure 5) and by citations to patient studies.

claim: Dystroglycan is composed of a cell-surface α-subunit and a transmembrane β-subunit.
source: DG is composed of a cell-surface α-subunit and a transmembrane β-subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dystroglycan structure.

claim: α-DG acts as a receptor for laminin-G domain-containing extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins such as laminin, agrin, perlecan and neurexin.
source: α-DG acts as a receptor for laminin-G domain-containing extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins such as laminin, agrin, perlecan and neurexin (Barresi and Campbell, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barresi and Campbell, 2006.

claim: α-DG serves as a cellular receptor and entry site for most Old World arenaviruses, including the highly pathogenic Lassa virus (LASV) and Clade C New Word arenaviruses.
source: In addition, it serves as a cellular receptor and entry site for most Old World arenaviruses, including the highly pathogenic Lassa virus (LASV) and Clade C New Word arenaviruses (Cao et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cao et al., 1998.

claim: LASV is the causative agent of severe hemorrhagic fever in humans with a mortality rate of ∼15% resulting in several thousand deaths each year.
source: LASV is the causative agent of severe hemorrhagic fever in humans, a disease that has a mortality rate of ∼15% resulting in several thousand deaths each year.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Lassa virus.

claim: A phosphorylated O-mannosyl glycan moiety in the N-terminal region of the α-DG mucin domain is essential for ligand binding.
source: Besides numerous modifications with N-glycans and mucin-type O-glycans, a highly complicated series of additions to a phosphorylated O-mannosyl glycan moiety in the N-terminal region of the mucin domain are essential for ligand binding (Kanagawa et al., 2004; Hara et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kanagawa et al., 2004 and Hara et al., 2011.

claim: Defects in the proper post-translational processing of α-DG result in loss of receptor function and in a broad spectrum of congenital muscular dystrophies (CMDs) accompanied by brain and eye malformations.
source: Defects in the proper post-translational processing of α-DG result in loss of receptor function, and in a broad spectrum of congenital muscular dystrophies (CMDs) that are accompanied by a variety of brain and eye malformations.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: These dystrophies are collectively classified as dystroglycanopathies.
source: Collectively, these dystrophies are classified as dystroglycanopathies (Barresi and Campbell, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barresi and Campbell, 2006.

claim: Over 17 genes have been reported to be directly or indirectly involved in functional glycosylation of α-DG and have been linked to human disease when mutated.
source: To date, over 17 genes have been reported to be directly or indirectly involved in this 'functional glycosylation' of α-DG, and have been linked to human disease when mutated (Mercuri and Muntoni, 2012; Bonnemann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mercuri and Muntoni, 2012 and Bonnemann et al., 2014.

claim: POMGNT2, B3GALNT2 and POMK contribute to the synthesis of a phosphorylated, O-mannosyl-linked trisaccharide on α-DG.
source: In our previous work we were able to assign functions to the POMGNT2 (Protein O-linked mannose N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 2) (GTDC2), B3GALNT2 and POMK (Protein O-mannose kinase) (SGK196) gene products, which contribute to the synthesis of a phosphorylated, O-mannosyl-linked trisaccharide on α-DG (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).

claim: The Core M3 structure (GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man-α Ser/Thr) is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: This so-called Core M3 structure (GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man-α Ser/Thr) is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work and established knowledge.

claim: The Core M3 structure is thought to be a platform for further functional modification of α-DG as it passes through the secretory pathway.
source: it is thought to be a platform for further functional modification of α-DG as it passes through the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is based on inference from the authors' previous work and current understanding.

claim: The glycosyltransferase LARGE synthesizes and transfers repeating units of [–3-xylose–α1,3-glucuronic acid-β1–] to α-DG.
source: The glycosyltransferase LARGE was shown to synthesize and transfer repeating units of [–3-xylose–α1,3-glucuronic acid-β1–] to α-DG (Inamori et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Inamori et al., 2012.

claim: The LARGE heteropolymer is postulated to be the terminal glycan moiety anchored by the Core M3 structure.
source: This heteropolymer is postulated to be the terminal glycan moiety anchored by the Core M3 structure.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on current understanding and inference.

claim: The LARGE heteropolymer resembles the ligand-binding glycan and its length correlates with the affinity of α-DG for its ligands.
source: It resembles the ligand-binding glycan and its length correlates with the affinity of α-DG for its ligands (Goddeeris et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goddeeris et al., 2013.

claim: Fibroblasts with defects in FKTN, FKRP, TMEM5, B4GAT1 and LARGE, but not in POMK, were able to produce radioactively labeled DGFc340.
source: In our experiment, fibroblasts with defects in FKTN, FKRP, TMEM5, B4GAT1 (B3GNT1) and LARGE, but not in the phosphate kinase POMK, were able to produce radioactively labeled DGFc340 (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: FKTN, FKRP, TMEM5, B4GAT1 and LARGE are involved downstream of POMK in the Core M3 post-phosphorylation process.
source: indicating that FKTN, FKRP, TMEM5, B4GAT1 and LARGE are involved downstream of POMK in the Core M3 post-phosphorylation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the phosphorylation data in Figure 1A.

claim: FKTN, FKRP, TMEM5, B4GAT1 and LARGE co-localize with the Golgi-resident marker protein Giantin.
source: Immunofluorescence examination of HEK293T (Human Embryonic Kidney) cells stably transfected with Myc-tagged constructs of this set of proteins, revealed that they co-localize with the Golgi-resident marker protein Giantin (Linstedt and Hauri, 1993) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most if not all of the α-DG O-mannosyl post-phosphoryl processing is carried out by Golgi-resident enzymes.
source: These results indicate that most if not all of the α-DG O-mannosyl post-phosphoryl processing is carried out by Golgi-resident enzymes.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data in Figure 1B.

claim: Overexpression of LARGE did not produce the IIH6-positive glycan or significantly bypass the glycosylation defect in FKTN-, FKRP-, TMEM5- or B4GAT1-deficient cells.
source: As expected, overexpression of LARGE did not produce the IIH6-positive glycan or significantly bypass the glycosylation defect in either FKTN-, FKRP-, TMEM5- or B4GAT1-deficient cells (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by On-Cell immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: FKTN, FKRP, TMEM5 and B4GAT1 work prior to LARGE in the O-mannosyl post-phosphoryl modification process.
source: supporting the notion that these encoded proteins work prior to LARGE in the O-mannosyl post-phosphoryl modification process.
evidence: This is inferred from the LARGE overexpression data in Figure 1C.

claim: Golgi-localized putative glycosyltransferases FKTN, FKRP, TMEM5 and B4GAT1 are essential for the synthesis of a linker structure that connects the α-DG O-mannosyl phosphate platform with the terminal laminin binding glycan added by LARGE.
source: In summary, our data suggest that Golgi-localized putative glycosyltransferases FKTN, FKRP, TMEM5 and B4GAT1 are essential for the synthesis of a linker structure that is connecting the α-DG O-mannosyl phosphate platform with the terminal laminin binding glycan added by LARGE.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: When [14C] UDP-Xyl and [14C] UDP-GlcA radionucleotides were tested individually in the LARGEdTM in vitro assay, the addition of [14C] UDP-Xyl, but not that of [14C] UDP-GlcA, resulted in radioactive labeling of the DGFc340 acceptor.
source: When the radionucleotide sugars were tested individually in the LARGEdTM in vitro assay, the addition of [14C] UDP-Xyl, but not that of [14C] UDP-GlcA radionucleotides, resulted in radioactive labeling of the DGFc340 acceptor (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by radioactive labeling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the presence of both UDP-Xyl and UDP-GlcA, the transfer of radioactivity was significantly increased.
source: However, in the presence of both UDP-Xyl and UDP-GlcA, the transfer of radioactivity was significantly increased consistent with the fact that the LARGE glycan is a heteropolysaccharide (Figure 2A/B).
evidence: This is supported by radioactive labeling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Xylose is the initial sugar transferred by LARGE, followed by the transfer of GlcA to form the repeating [–3-xylose–α1,3-glucuronic acid-β1–] heteropolymer.
source: These results indicate that xylose is the initial sugar transferred by LARGE, and that this is followed by the transfer of GlcA to form the repeating [–3-xylose–α1,3-glucuronic acid-β1–] heteropolymer.
evidence: This is inferred from the radioactive labeling data in Figure 2B.

claim: Pretreatment of Largemyd DGFc340 with β-glucuronidase resulted in a strong reduction of the IIH6 signal.
source: Subsequent immunoblotting with the LARGE glycan-specific antibody (IIH6) revealed that the pretreatment of Largemyd DGFc340 with β-glucuronidase resulted in a strong reduction of the IIH6 signal (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: LARGE uses a β-linked GlcA residue as an acceptor sugar to initiate synthesis of the polymeric glycan.
source: These data indicate that LARGE uses a β-linked GlcA residue as an acceptor sugar to initiate synthesis of the polymeric glycan.
evidence: This is inferred from the β-glucuronidase treatment data in Figure 2C.

claim: LARGEdTM was able to efficiently modify DGFc340 from Pro5 (wild-type), Lec2 (CMP-sialic acid-deficient), Lec8 (UDP-galactose-deficient) and Lec13 (GDP-fucose-deficient) cells.
source: LARGEdTM was able to efficiently modify DGFc340 from Pro5 (wild-type), Lec2 (CMP-sialic acid-deficient), Lec8 (UDP-galactose-deficient) and Lec13 (GDP-fucose-deficient) cells, suggesting that sialic acid, galactose and fucose do not contribute to functional glycosylation of α-DG (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sialic acid, galactose and fucose do not contribute to functional glycosylation of α-DG.
source: suggesting that sialic acid, galactose and fucose do not contribute to functional glycosylation of α-DG (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DGFc340 from UDP-Xyl-deficient pgsI-208 CHO cells was not modified by LARGEdTM in the in vitro assay.
source: Most interestingly, in the LARGEdTM in vitro assay DGFc340 from UDP-Xyl-deficient pgsI-208 CHO cells was not modified (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: One or more xylose residues are required on α-DG before it can be functionally glycosylated by LARGE.
source: This clearly demonstrated that one or more xylose residues are required on α-DG before it can be functionally glycosylated by LARGE (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the pgsI-208 data in Figure 2D.

claim: B4GAT1 shares 44% similarity with the LARGE GlcA-T (Glucuronyltransferase) domain.
source: In particular it shares 44% similarity with the LARGE GlcA-T (Glucuronyltransferase) domain (CAZy: GT49; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: A unique product peak was detected only when UDP-GlcA was used as donor in the B4GAT1dTM transfer assay.
source: A unique product peak was detected only when UDP-GlcA was used as donor (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: B4GAT1dTM GlcA-T activity has low preference for α-linked Xyl, but showed >10-fold higher preference and specificity towards β-linked Xyl acceptors.
source: We also tested the acceptor specificity, which revealed that B4GAT1dTM GlcA-T activity has low preference for α-linked Xyl, but showed >10- fold higher preference and specificity towards β-linked Xyl acceptors (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The LARGE glycan disaccharide Xyl-α1,3-GlcA-MU was a very weak acceptor for B4GAT1dTM GlcA-transfer.
source: The fact that the LARGE glycan disaccharide Xyl-α1,3-GlcA-MU was a very weak acceptor for B4GAT1dTM GlcA-transfer suggests that B4GAT1 overexpression does not interfere with LARGE mediated synthesis of the laminin-binding glycan.
evidence: This is inferred from the acceptor specificity data in Figure 3C.

claim: B4GAT1 GlcA-T activity has a metal dependence for manganese (Mn2+) divalent cations.
source: A characterization of the B4GAT1 GlcA-T activity revealed a metal dependence for manganese (Mn2+) divalent cations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: B4GAT1 GlcA-T activity has a pH-optimum near pH 7.0.
source: and a pH-optimum near pH 7.0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The GlcA residue transferred by B4GAT1dTM was β-linked to the four position of the xylose β-MU.
source: The product peak obtained from the enzymatic reaction of B4GAT1dTM with β-Xyl-MU acceptor was isolated, and its analysis by NMR revealed that the GlcA residue was β-linked to the four position of the xylose β-MU (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by NMR structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: B4GAT1 possesses xylose β1,4-glucuronyltransferase (GlcA-T) activity and it is specific for the substrate β-linked Xyl.
source: Thus, B4GAT1 possesses xylose β1,4-glucuronyltransferase (GlcA-T) activity and it is specific for the substrate β-linked Xyl.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the enzyme activity and NMR data in Figure 3.

claim: LARGE did not distinguish between GlcA-β1,3-Xyl and GlcA-β1,4-Xyl, as similar activities were measured in the presence of both disaccharide acceptors.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, LARGE did not distinguish between GlcA-β1,3-Xyl and GlcA-β1,4-Xyl, as similar activities were measured in the presence of both disaccharide acceptors.
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The disaccharide acceptor showed 25-fold higher activity than the monosaccharide acceptor for LARGE Xyl-T.
source: However, the length of the acceptor appears to be important, since the disaccharide acceptor showed 25-fold higher activity than the monosaccharide acceptor (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Control MEFs were positive for functional glycosylation of, and laminin-binding by, α-DG.
source: Immunoblotting revealed that whereas control MEFs were positive for functional glycosylation of, and laminin-binding by, α-DG
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: α-DG from Largemyd MEFs completely lacked functional glycosylation and laminin binding.
source: from Largemyd MEFs completely lacked both features (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: B4gat1-deficient MEFs demonstrated strongly reduced but detectable residual functional glycosylation and laminin binding.
source: Also, B4gat1-deficient MEFs demonstrated strongly reduced but detectable residual functional glycosylation and laminin binding, and normal levels of hypoglycosylated α-DG core protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Adenovirus-mediated ectopic expression of B4GAT1 was able to rescue the α-DG glycosylation defect in B4gat1-deficient MEFs.
source: Adenovirus-mediated ectopic expression of B4GAT1 did not affect the glycosylation status of α-DG in control and Largemyd MEFs but, as expected, was able to rescue the α-DG glycosylation defect in B4gat1-deficient MEFs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: B4gat1-deficient cells showed only a low level of α-DG hyperglycosylation after LARGE overexpression.
source: In contrast, B4gat1-deficient cells showed only a low level of α-DG hyperglycosylation after LARGE overexpression (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the context of mutant B4GAT1, only few acceptor sites for LARGE modification are available.
source: suggesting that in the context of mutant B4GAT1, only few acceptor sites for LARGE modification are available.
evidence: This is inferred from the LARGE overexpression data in Figure 4A.

claim: Ectopic co-expression of B4GAT1 and LARGE resulted in α-DG hyperglycosylation in all three tested MEF lines.
source: Finally, ectopic co-expression of B4GAT1 and LARGE resulted in α-DG hyperglycosylation in all three tested MEF lines (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: B4GAT1 acts prior to the glycosyltransferase LARGE.
source: This result is consistent with the hypothesis that B4GAT1 acts prior to the glycosyltransferase LARGE.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation data in Figure 4A.

claim: Control and Largemyd samples showed comparable B4GAT1 transferase activity.
source: Whereas control and Largemyd samples showed comparable B4GAT1 transferase activity, only low residual activity (<3%) was detectable in B4gat1-deficient cells, and this loss could be restored by ectopic expression of B4GAT1 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A/B).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only low residual activity (<3%) was detectable in B4gat1-deficient cells.
source: only low residual activity (<3%) was detectable in B4gat1-deficient cells
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only Largemyd MEFs lacked LARGE GlcA-T activity; the control and B4gat1-deficient cells were normal.
source: Similarly, when we tested LARGE GlcA-T activity in control and glycosylation-deficient MEFs, only Largemyd MEFs lacked LARGE GlcA-T activity; the control and B4gat1-deficient cells were normal (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C/D).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The enzymatic activities of B4GAT1 and LARGE are independent and each is unaffected by mutations in the gene product of the other.
source: These results suggest that the enzymatic activities of B4GAT1 and LARGE are independent and that each is unaffected by mutations in the gene product of the other.
evidence: This is inferred from the enzyme activity data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Expression levels were similar for the Myc-tagged B4GAT1 control and all three mutant constructs Mut1-Mut3 in stably expressing HEK293T cells.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed that expression levels were similar for the Myc-tagged B4GAT1 control and all three mutant constructs Mut1-Mut3 in stably expressing HEK293T cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both the control and mutant construct Mut1 exhibit normal Golgi localization and co-localize with the Golgi marker Giantin.
source: In our immunofluorescence analysis, we found both the control and mutant construct Mut1 to exhibit normal Golgi localization and to co-localize with the Golgi marker Giantin (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: B4GAT1 mutations in constructs Mut2 and Mut3 resulted in a high degree of mislocalization to the ER.
source: B4GAT1 mutations in constructs Mut2 and Mut3, however, resulted in a high degree of mislocalization to the ER, as judged by overlap of the signal with the ER marker ERp72 (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The B4GAT1 mutant proteins Mut2 and Mut3 are misfolded and retained in the ER.
source: indicating that the B4GAT1 mutant proteins are misfolded and retained in the ER.
evidence: This is inferred from the mislocalization data in Figure 5D.

claim: All three B4GAT1 mutants showed strongly reduced activity of less than 5% compared to activity levels in wild-type control.
source: Analysis of B4GAT1 enzyme activity in lysates from cells stably overexpressing these constructs revealed strongly reduced activity in the cases of all three mutants, of less than 5% compared to activity levels in wild-type control (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: None of the B4GAT1 mutant constructs was able to complement and rescue the α-DG glycosylation defect in B4gat1-deficient MEFs.
source: Similarly, none of the B4GAT1 mutant constructs was able to complement and rescue the α-DG glycosylation defect in B4gat1-deficient MEFs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The identified B4GAT1 mutations are pathological and have a direct negative impact on B4GAT1 activity regardless of their subcellular localization.
source: These findings confirm that the identified B4GAT1 mutations are pathological and have a direct negative impact on B4GAT1 activity regardless of their subcellular localization.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the mutation analysis data in Figure 5.

claim: The B4GAT1 DXD motif is essential.
source: Additionally, the finding that the B4GAT1 DXD motif is essential further supports a role for B4GAT1 as a glycosyltransferase
evidence: This is inferred from the Mut2 (DXD motif mutation) data in Figure 5.

claim: The DXD motif is thought to be involved in binding carbohydrate sugar-nucleoside diphosphates in manganese-dependent glycosyltransferases.
source: since the DXD motif is thought to be involved in binding carbohydrate sugar-nucleoside diphosphates in manganese-dependent glycosyltransferases (Wiggins and Munro, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wiggins and Munro, 1998.

claim: DGFc340 isolated from B4gat1-deficient cells was the only acceptor that incorporated substantial levels of the radioactive label in the B4GAT1dTM assay.
source: As expected, DGFc340 isolated from B4gat1-deficient cells was the only acceptor that incorporated substantial levels of the radioactive label (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by radioactive labeling data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: After β-xylosidase treatment, the ability of B4gat1-deficient DGFc340 to act as an acceptor was strongly reduced.
source: After β-xylosidase treatment, the ability of B4gat1-deficient DGFc340 to act as an acceptor was strongly reduced; this constitutes indirect evidence that a β-linked xylose is indeed the postulated endogenous acceptor for B4GAT1 (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is supported by β-xylosidase treatment data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A β-linked xylose is the postulated endogenous acceptor for B4GAT1.
source: this constitutes indirect evidence that a β-linked xylose is indeed the postulated endogenous acceptor for B4GAT1 (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is inferred from the β-xylosidase treatment data in Figure 6B.

claim: A yet unidentified xylosyltransferase acts upstream of B4GAT1.
source: and that a yet unidentified xylosyltransferase acts upstream of B4GAT1.
evidence: This is inferred from the β-xylosidase treatment data in Figure 6B.

claim: The tetrasaccharide has the glycosidic linkage structure GlcA-β1,3-Xyl-α1,3-GlcA-β1,4-Xyl-β-MU.
source: Therefore, the tetrasaccharide has the glycosidic linkage structure GlcA-β1,3-Xyl-α1,3-GlcA-β1,4-Xyl-β-MU (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by NMR structural analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: B4GAT1 possesses β1,4 glucuronyltransferase activity.
source: These studies show that B4GAT1 possesses β1,4 glucuronyltransferase activity
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the NMR data in Figure 7.

claim: LARGE can elongate the B4GAT1 primer structure by adding repeating units [-3-Xyl-α1,3-GlcA-β1-] to produce a heteropolysaccharide.
source: and that LARGE can elongate this primer structure by adding repeating units [-3-Xyl-α1,3-GlcA-β1-] to produce a heteropolysaccharide.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the NMR data in Figure 7.

claim: B4GAT1 was initially cloned and described by Sasaki et al. as β1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (iGnT, β3GNT1 or B3GNT1).
source: B4GAT1 was initially cloned and described by Sasaki et al., (Sasaki et al., 1997) as β1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase (iGnT, β3GNT1 or B3GNT1)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sasaki et al., 1997.

claim: The B3GNT1 enzyme was proposed to contribute to the i antigen synthesis pathway by transferring N-acetylglucosamine onto a β-galactose acceptor with β1,3 linkage.
source: Furthermore, the B3GNT1 enzyme was proposed to contribute to the i antigen synthesis pathway by transferring N-acetylglucosamine onto a β-galactose acceptor with β1,3 linkage (Sasaki et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sasaki et al., 1997.

claim: The authors' data reveal a β1,4-glucuronyltransferase activity for B4GAT1.
source: In contrast our data reveal a β1,4-glucuronyltransferase activity, which we have designated B4GAT1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the enzyme activity and NMR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors were not able to validate any N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase activity for B4GAT1dTM with UDP-GlcNAc and the proposed Gal-β1,4-GlcNAc-β-MU acceptor.
source: We tested B4GAT1dTM with UDP-GlcNAc and the proposed Gal-β1,4-GlcNAc-β-MU acceptor, but we were not able to validate any N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Only 2 other enzymes are known to have β1,4-glucuronyltransferase activity: EXT1 and EXT2.
source: To date, only 2 other enzymes are known to have β1,4-glucuronyltransferase activity. These are EXT1 and EXT2, and both are involved in the synthesis of heparan sulphate proteoglycans (Lidholt and Lindahl, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lidholt and Lindahl, 1992.

claim: EXT1 and EXT2 are involved in the synthesis of heparan sulphate proteoglycans.
source: These are EXT1 and EXT2, and both are involved in the synthesis of heparan sulphate proteoglycans (Lidholt and Lindahl, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lidholt and Lindahl, 1992.

claim: The findings regarding assembly of the LARGE glycan reveal striking similarities to the unique mechanism underlying the synthesis of proteoglycans.
source: Our findings regarding assembly of the LARGE glycan reveal striking similarities to the unique mechanism underlying the synthesis of proteoglycans.
evidence: This is a comparison and inference based on the authors' findings and established knowledge.
